title: How fast things vanish
hook: how quickly all things disappear, bodies and memories alike (Meditations 2.12)

segments.voice: Yesterday: ready to leave, the bag half packed. Your line was ready. What did you do that you'd hate to leave undone? Day five hundred thirty-six.

Go back to the street where you grew up, and the corner store is a phone shop. The teacher who scared you is long retired. The song everyone knew that summer, nobody under twenty has heard of. Scroll back far enough in your own photos and there are faces you can't name anymore. It happens so gradually that it's only when you look back that you see it. In section twelve, Marcus looks back, and looks hard, and starts with a sentence that's almost a sigh. Today: how fast things vanish.
screen: `THE CORNER STORE IS GONE.` → `FACES YOU CAN'T NAME.` → `HOW FAST THINGS VANISH.`

segments.voice: First, two kinds of vanishing. How quickly everything disappears, Marcus says: bodies, out of the world, and then the memory of them, out of time. First the person goes. Then, more slowly, the remembering goes. Second, what dazzles. Then he looks at the things that pull at us hardest: things that tempt with pleasure, things that frighten with pain, things people brag about. How cheap they are, he says, how perishable, how quickly gone. It's the same trick we've seen on this path with the emperor's purple robe, looking at something until its glamour wears off. Third, death itself. And what is dying? If you look at it alone, he says, stripping away all the imaginings we pile onto it, you'll see it's simply a work of nature. And to be terrified of a work of nature is, in his words, to be like a child. He doesn't mean grief is childish. He means the dread we add on top of the plain fact. Fourth, what's near. The entry ends with a question, not an answer: how does a human being touch God, and by what part of himself, and when? For Marcus, the answer was the ruling part, the reasoning mind we met a few days ago. Readers on other paths will name it differently, or not at all. But the turn is worth noticing. After everything that vanishes, he points at what's closest. Not to escape the vanishing. To stand in it, steadily, and say: so quickly. And then, still, to live today.
screen: `BODIES GO; THEN MEMORIES GO.` · `WHAT DAZZLES IS PERISHABLE.` · `DEATH: A WORK OF NATURE.` · `WHAT PART OF US TOUCHES GOD?` · then, large: `SO QUICKLY.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing that's already gone. A place, a voice, a habit, a version of yourself from ten years ago. Let yourself see it clearly for a moment. Notice how quickly it went, and how it still lives a little in you. Don't hurry past the feeling. Then come back to this breath, here, which is also going, and is still here. The bell holds the time.
How fast things vanish. Marcus: bodies leave the world, and then their memory leaves time, so quickly. Death, seen plainly, is a work of nature. Today's word.
Your line: so quickly. Once today, look at something ordinary, a mug, a face, the light, and say inside: so quickly. Then enjoy it. Day five hundred thirty-six.

howItsDone: Many people practicing Stoicism reflect regularly on impermanence, letting it loosen the grip of status and pleasure and sharpen their attention to the present.

fork.reveal: look at it alone, Marcus says, without the imaginings, and you'll see a work of nature.

original.note: Greek: nature. For Marcus, dying is 'a work of nature', nothing more frightening than that.

trapdoor: what you thought: everything dies, so why bother?
what it means: see plainly how fast things go, strip off the dread, and stand steady in the present.
what a scholar hears: 2.12 runs a Stoic 'physics' exercise, analyzing objects into what they are, then ends on the soul's kinship with God.

notes: Meditations 2.12 paraphrased: how quickly all things disappear, bodies in the universe and their remembrance in time; objects of sense that allure with pleasure or terrify with pain or are noised abroad by vanity, how worthless and perishable; death, looked at alone without imaginings, is an operation of nature, and to fear it is childish; how man is near to God, by what part, and when. Confirm.
